title: Running an AI assistant without internet
excerpt: Survival LLM lets a free, open-source AI answer emergency questions entirely offline on your computer.
body:
A recent test ran 22 blackout and first-aid questions against Survival LLM and the model got the main point right on every one, even though it never contacts the internet.

The app lives entirely on the computer, pulls the AI model that matches the available RAM, and answers from a library that includes FEMA guidance, CDC articles, and about 930 000 Wikipedia entries. The result is an assistant that can still tell you how to purify water or treat a burn when the network is down.

The post shows how the offline model adapts to your hardware, what sources power the answers, and how to manage storage, power and updates. By the end you’ll know the steps to get a self-contained AI assistant up and running on any recent Windows or macOS machine.

## How the offline model adapts to your hardware

When the app launches it checks the computer’s memory and downloads the AI model that fits. More RAM means a larger, smarter model; less RAM triggers a smaller model that still works but makes more mistakes. The source notes that “smaller models make more mistakes, so the app always shows the source to check.” This adaptive download happens only once, during the initial online setup.

Because the model is stored locally, the size of the model plus a 5 GB buffer determines the minimum free disk space. On an Apple Silicon Mac with macOS 14 or a 64-bit Windows 10/11 machine, the app selects the appropriate binary and model automatically. No manual selection is required, which keeps the process simple for users who are not comfortable tweaking model parameters.

## What sources power the answers

Every answer lists the articles it read, and each article can be opened with the exact passage highlighted. The library combines several openly licensed collections:

* About 930 000 of Wikipedia’s most-read articles  
* MedlinePlus from the U.S. National Library of Medicine  
* UK Medicines A-to-Z (public sector information)  
* U.S. military medicine and survival manuals  
* Home-repair, cooking, gardening and ham-radio Q&A from Stack Exchange  

Each source keeps its own license, which the app shows alongside the article. The system also lets you add PDFs, Word documents, e-books and personal notes, letting the AI search those files without ever leaving the computer.

Because the answer always cites its source, users can verify the guidance themselves. In the blackout test, the model’s “right” rating came from this transparent citation practice, not from hidden internet queries.

## Managing storage, power and updates

The full library is a 9 GB download (19 GB once installed). A lighter version without Wikipedia and iFixit is 1.3 GB (3 GB installed). During installation the app needs about 27 GB of free space for the full set and 10 GB for the smaller set. After installation the permanent footprint is the model size plus 5 GB.

Power consumption is modest. On a MacBook Pro the app measured about 100 W while answering, taking 5 to 40 seconds per question. That translates to roughly 100 to 300 answers on a full battery, and a small generator or portable power station can run it easily.

Updates are handled inside the app. Clicking “Check for updates” at the bottom downloads a new version in one click and replaces the models, library and any added files. The process works offline after the initial download, because the update package is fetched only when the user is online.

## The takeaway

Set up Survival LLM while you have internet, then let it run without a connection. The app automatically picks a model that matches your RAM, cites openly licensed sources for every answer, and runs on modest power. Verify guidance by opening the listed articles, and keep the system current with the built-in update button.
